articles.title: DEEP SKY OBSERVING
articles.summary: This document provides a deep-sky observing list curated by Mark Wagner for November 2007, focusing on the period from the third quarter to the new moon. It details various celestial objects, including galaxies, planetary nebulae, and open clusters, primarily located in northern constellations like Cepheus, Cassiopeia, Perseus, and Andromeda. Each entry includes astronomical data and specific observational notes for amateur astronomers.

articles.title: Mars Going Backwards
articles.summary: This article explains Mars's upcoming retrograde motion starting November 15, an apparent westward movement on a star chart. Historically, this phenomenon caused complexity for geocentric models like Ptolemy's epicycles, but Copernicus and Kepler simplified the explanation: it's an optical illusion caused by Earth's position and faster orbit as it overtakes an outer planet like Mars. Retrograde motion typically occurs near a planet's opposition.

articles.title: The Shallow Sky
articles.summary: The 'Shallow Sky' article offers an astronomical observing guide for November 2007, detailing optimal viewing for Mars (nearing opposition), Jupiter (including a rare double shadow transit on Nov 4th), Saturn, Venus, Mercury, and the asteroid Ceres. It also highlights a lunar occultation of Regulus on Nov 2-3. Additionally, the article announces a free public lecture by Jeff Moore of NASA Ames on November 13, 2007, covering discoveries from the New Horizons mission at Jupiter and the Cassini mission at Saturn.

articles.title: A Missile in Your Eye
articles.summary: JPL scientists, initially developing a rapid spectrometer (CTIS) to detect ballistic missile launches, are now adapting this "missile-quick" technology for medical applications. This spectrometer can capture the entire retina's spectral information in a 3-millisecond snapshot, allowing doctors to detect low oxygen levels—an indicator of eye disease—despite constant eye movement. Clinical trials are underway for this relatively inexpensive spin-off technology.

articles.title: The Last 31 Days In Astronomy
articles.summary: This astronomy news compilation from September-October 2007 highlights several significant events: the Mars rover Opportunity reaching Victoria Crater, the launch of the Dawn spacecraft to Vesta and Ceres, and the inauguration of the Allen Telescope Array (ATA-42). Other notable reports include a significant reduction in Arctic sea ice, revised measurements for the Orion Nebula's distance and age, detailed imaging of Mercury using 'lucky imaging' technique, a new crew for the International Space Station, and the discovery of a rare CO2 isotope affecting atmospheric models for Venus and Mars.

articles.title: Astronomical Swap Meet November 18, 2007
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) is hosting its annual astronomical swap meet on Sunday, November 18, 2007, at Houge Park in San Jose. This event allows individuals to buy, sell, and trade astronomy-related equipment and literature, operating as a club fundraiser with a 10% donation requested on sales. The swap meet will feature a consignment table for sellers with few items and encourages community participation.
